summary: Defines two LDAP controls, one in the bind request and one in the response, that let a client ask which authorization identity the server decided to give it after authentication. This helps when the identity differs from the name the client supplied.

plainLanguage.summary: After you show your badge at the door, you can ask the guard, "Who exactly do you think I am?" and get an answer.

subtitle: Two LDAP bind controls that let a client ask the server which identity it was actually granted.

tldr.problem: After an LDAP bind, the server may map the identity the client presented (a certificate, say) to a different directory identity, and the client has no way to learn which one it got.
tldr.mechanism: The client attaches an Authorization Identity Request Control, with no value, to its bind request. On success the server answers with an Authorization Identity Response Control that carries the granted authzId.
tldr.outcome: The client can see its granted identity right in the bind response, without an extra operation. The identity travels outside any security layer the bind sets up, so sensitive deployments should secure the channel first.

today: RFC 3829 is an Informational RFC. The unit metadata shows no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why a Client Wants to Know Its Identity
sections.content:
RFC 3829 defines two controls for the LDAP bind operation: the Authorization Identity Request Control and the Authorization Identity Response Control. A client sends the first in a bind request; the server may reply with the second in its bind response. The response holds the identity the client was granted.

This helps when the server maps or redirects identities during the bind. Client authentication with certificates is the main case. Some SASL mechanisms also leave out an explicit DN, or end with an authorization identity that differs from the authentication identity the client supplied. The request control may only be used with LDAP version 3.
sections.plainLanguage: Sometimes the guard lets you in under a different name than the one on your badge. These controls let you ask which name you were given.

sections.title: The Request and Response Controls
sections.content:
The request control MAY go in any bind request that specifies protocol version 3, in the controls field of the LDAPMessage. Its controlType is 2.16.840.1.113730.3.4.16 and its controlValue is absent. In a multi-step bind, the client MUST send the control with each bind request.

The response control MAY appear in the final bind response, if the first bind request of the bind carried the request control. Its controlType is 2.16.840.1.113730.3.4.15. On success with a non-anonymous identity, the controlValue holds the authorization identity (authzId) granted. For an anonymous association it is a zero-length string. If the bind produced more than one authzId, the primary one is returned.

The response control is only included when the bind's resultCode is success.
sections.plainLanguage: You ask with a blank note. The answer comes back on a note with your name on it, or a blank note if you are just a guest.

sections.title: Failure Cases and a Certificate Example
sections.content:
If the server requires confidentiality protections before using the control and they are missing, it returns the confidentialityRequired result code. If the client lacks access rights to the authorization information, the server returns insufficientAccessRights.

The RFC's example: a client holding several certificates may not know which one the server chose, and the certificate's subject DN may not match a directory DN exactly because the server maps it. After certificate authentication, the client can send a SASL bind using the EXTERNAL mechanism with the request control. The response MAY then name the DN in the server's Directory Information Tree that the certificate was mapped to.
sections.plainLanguage: If the guard says the answer is private, or you are not allowed to ask, you get a polite refusal instead of a name.

sections.title: The "Who am I?" Alternative
sections.content:
The LDAP "Who am I?" extended operation can also report the authorization identity of a bound connection. Because it runs after the bind, it lets a client learn the identity once integrity and confidentiality protections are in place. Its drawbacks are the need to coordinate it with bind and other requests, and the extra operation required.

For multithreaded or high-bandwidth server environments, the RFC says the bind response approach may be preferable.
sections.plainLanguage: You can also ask "Who am I?" later, after you are inside. That takes one more question, but the room can already be private.

sections.title: Security and IANA Considerations
sections.content:
The controls are subject to standard LDAP security considerations and may be sent over a secure or an insecure channel. They are not protected by security layers negotiated by the bind operation.

Because the response can pass an additional authorization identity, which in some deployments may be confidential, the RFC says a security layer should be established before issuing a bind request with the request control. Support is advertised by listing the two OIDs in the supportedControl attribute of the server's root DSE. The OIDs are reserved for these controls, and the request control is registered as an LDAP Protocol Mechanism.
sections.plainLanguage: The answer slip is not locked in a safe. If your name is a secret, set up a private room before you ask.

messages.label: Bind response + Response Control
messages.note: Control type 2.16.840.1.113730.3.4.15, value is the authzId; only sent when the result is success.
